Numidia: Kingdom in North Africa, 202 to 25 BC.
A West Point-trained engineer, this Confederate general fired the opening shots of the American Civil War at Fort Sumter — yet signed his letters "G. T.," rarely using his first name. Who was he?
P. G. T. Beauregard: Confederate States Army general (1818–1893)
Abducted by her uncle Hades and made queen of the underworld, this daughter of Zeus and Demeter personifies the return of spring each year — who is she?
Persephone: Greek goddess of spring and the queen of the underworld.

After eight years in UN-funded public health work, this Indian strategist helped re-elect Narendra Modi as Gujarat's chief minister in 2012 before founding his own party ahead of the 2025 Bihar election — who is he?
Prashant Kishor: Indian politician. Prashant Kishor (born 20 March 1977), colloquially known as PK, is an Indian politician, the founder of the Jan Suraaj Party and a former political strategist.
This Indian politician became Minister of Defence in 2019 and was the first person born after independence to serve as Union Minister of Home Affairs — who is he?
Rajnath Singh: Defense Minister of India since 2019.
Going by his initials 'rms,' this programmer launched the GNU Project, founded the Free Software Foundation, and wrote every version of the GNU General Public License — who is he?
Richard Stallman: American activist and programmer (born 1953)
Orphaned of his murdered father at age two, this Shia cleric grew up to lead a revolution that toppled the Shah and made him his country's first supreme leader — who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini: Supreme Leader of Iran from 1979 to 1989.
A moderate conservative swing vote nominated by Ronald Reagan, this former Arizona state judge made history in 1981 as the first woman on the U.S. Supreme Court — who is it?
Sandra Day O'Connor: American lawyer, politician and judge (1930–2023)
This Russian nihilist preached revolution "by any means necessary" and fled the country in 1869 after taking part in the murder of a former comrade who'd dared to disagree with him — who was he?

Sparked in 1991 when the Revolutionary United Front — backed by Liberia's Charles Taylor — moved to topple the Momoh government, this nearly 11-year conflict displaced some 2.5 million people. Which war is it?
Sierra Leone Civil War: 1991–2002 war in West Africa.
Son of a Greek Catholic priest in Galicia, he led a radical faction of Ukrainian nationalists and orchestrated the 1934 assassination of a Polish interior minister — who was he?
Serving as Ottoman Grand Vizier during World War I, this convicted war criminal is remembered as the architect of the Armenian genocide — who was he?
One of 24 Apollo astronauts to fly to the Moon, he commanded Apollo 10 and, with his crewmate, became the first to fly a Lunar Module in lunar orbit — which test pilot?
Thomas P. Stafford: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1930–2024)
As chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority, this Royal Court adviser also owned Spanish club Almería from 2019 to 2025 — who is he?
A free-love advocate and women's rights activist, she ran for president of the United States in 1872 — widely cited as the first woman to do so; who was she?
Victoria Woodhull: American women's suffrage activist (1838–1927)
Sparked by a dispute over Maria Theresa's right to inherit the Habsburg throne, this 1740–1748 conflict began when Prussia seized the wealthy province of Silesia — what was this conflict called?
War of the Austrian Succession: 1740–1748 war between European powers.

Known as the 'Mother of the Nation,' this South African anti-apartheid activist and politician served in parliament and led the ANC Women's League after marrying the country's future president in 1958 — who is she?
Winnie Mandela: South African activist and politician (1936–2018)

After helping secure the Qing dynasty's abdication, this Chinese general became the Republic's first formal president, only to declare himself emperor in 1915 and abdicate again months later — who was he?
Yuan Shikai: First president of the Republic of China (1859–1916)
Which of these people was born first?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Who among these was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Tycho Brahe is an astronomer. In 1572, Tycho noticed a completely new star that was brighter than any star or planet.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Robert Aumann is a mathematician. Aumann received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2005 for his work on conflict and cooperation through game theory analysis.
What is the atomic number of Molybdenum?
Molybdenum: Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
What is the atomic number of Iron?
Iron: Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
In what year was Neil Armstrong born?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year was Lewis Carroll born?
Lewis Carroll: An avid puzzler, Carroll created the word ladder puzzle, which he called "Doublets", which was published in Vanity Fair magazine between 1879 and 1881.
In what year was Mileva Marić born?
Mileva Marić: Marić and Einstein were study colleagues and lovers, and had a daughter Lieserl in 1902, who likely died of scarlet fever at one and a half years old.
In what year did Jane Goodall die?
Jane Goodall: Dame Valerie Jane Morris Goodall ( GUUD-awl; née Morris-Goodall; 3 April 1934 – 1 October 2025) was an English primatologist and anthropologist.
In what year did Carl Friedrich Gauss die?
Carl Friedrich Gauss: Gauss was director of the Göttingen Observatory in Germany and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855.
In what year was Klinefelter syndrome discovered?
Klinefelter syndrome: Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosome anomaly.
Bash (Unix shell): Brian Fox. Bash (short for "Bourne Again SHell") is an interactive command interpreter and command language developed for Unix-like operating systems.
Airbus A220: Bombardier Aerospace. The Airbus A220 is a family of five-abreast narrow-body airliners by Airbus Canada Limited Partnership (ACLP).
In which country is Mitsubishi A6M Zero?
Mitsubishi A6M Zero: Japan. It was operated by the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN) from 1940 to 1945.
Who is credited with discovering Malaria?
Malaria: Ronald Ross. Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease that is transmitted by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes.
Who is credited with discovering Kwashiorkor?
Kwashiorkor: Cicely Williams. Kwashiorkor ( KWOSH-ee-OR-kor, -⁠kər) is a form of severe protein malnutrition characterized by edema and an enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates.
Who is credited with discovering Titanium?
Titanium: William Gregor. Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Despite the conspiracy buzz, this violet compound is mass-produced, sold to the public, and not a controlled substance — its hemostatic derivative is carbazochrome. What is it?
Adrenochrome is a chemical compound produced by the oxidation of adrenaline (epinephrine).
This white crystalline chemical compound is mainly used as a high-nitrogen agricultural fertilizer, but is also a key ingredient in explosive mixtures used for mining and quarrying — what is it?
Ammonium nitrate is a chemical compound with the formula NH4NO3.
This emotion is defined by dread over events that haven't happened yet, distinguishing it from fear, which responds to a threat that's already present. What is it?
Anxiety is an emotion characterized by an unpleasant state of inner turmoil and includes feelings of dread over anticipated events.
Part of the family Ericaceae, these shrubs flower in April and May in the Northern Hemisphere and October and November south of the equator — what are they called?
Azalea (-) are flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron, particularly the former subgenera Tsutsusi (evergreen) and Pentanthera (deciduous).
This red-orange compound, formed from the breakdown of heme, is further processed into pigments that give feces their brown color and urine its straw-yellow hue. What is it?
Bilirubin (BR) (adopted from German, originally bili, for bile, plus ruber, Latin for red) is a red-orange compound that occurs as the reduction product of biliverdin, a breakdown product of heme.

Making up only about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and regulates critical functions like heart rate and breathing. What is it called?
Brainstem (or brain stem) is the posterior stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.
This biological family includes domestic dogs, wolves, coyotes, foxes, and jackals, found on every continent except Antarctica. What family is it?
Canidae (from Latin, canis, "dog") is a biological family of caniform carnivorans, constituting a clade.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
This neurological disorder strikes one side of the head around the eye and temple, often at the very same hour each day for an 8-to-10-week stretch before vanishing for months — what condition is it?
Cluster headache is a neurological disorder characterized by episodes of severe headaches on one side of the head, typically around the eye and temple, lasting between 15 minutes to three hours.
Which genus of passerine birds, whose Latin name literally means 'raven,' includes about 46 species commonly known as crows, ravens, and rooks?
Corvus is a widely distributed genus of passerine birds ranging from medium-sized to large-sized in the family Corvidae.
Affecting some 280 million people worldwide, this state of low mood saps motivation and the pleasure once taken in activities — what is it?
Depression (mood) is a mental state of low mood and aversion to activity.

This hypothetical megastructure would encircle an entire star to capture most of its energy output, conceived as a thought experiment for how an advanced civilization might meet growing power needs — what's the concept called?
Dyson sphere is a hypothetical megastructure that encompasses a star and captures a large percentage of its power output.
With a US prevalence of about 8.2 cases per million births, this inherited disorder can cause complications from esophageal narrowing to skin cancer to amputation — which condition?
Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is a group of rare medical conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.
A Swiss linguist and philosopher who died in 1913, this thinker's ideas shaped 20th-century linguistics, psychoanalysis, and anthropology alike, according to one of his translators — who is he?
Ferdinand de Saussure (26 November 1857 - 22 February 1913) was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher.
Its name comes from Greek for 'milk flower,' and this small genus of about 20 bulbous perennials nods with a single white bell of six tepals — what is the botanical name for the snowdrop?
Galanthus (from Ancient Greek, (gla, "milk") + (nthos, "flower")), or snowdrop, is a small genus of approximately 20 species of bulbous perennial herbaceous plants in the family Amaryllidaceae.

Found in northern South America, this tarantula is the world's heaviest and longest-bodied spider, tipping the scales at over 170 grams, though a huntsman spider still beats it on leg span — what spider is it?
Goliath birdeater (Theraphosa blondi) is a large spider that belongs to the tarantula family Theraphosidae.
This daisy-family genus native to North America and Mexico includes the common sunflower and the Jerusalem artichoke among its roughly 50 species — which genus?
Helianthus is a genus comprising around 50 species of annual and perennial flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae commonly known as sunflowers.
This semi-synthetic opioid, often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, treats severe pain and also suppresses cough — what drug is it?
Hydrocodone is a semi-synthetic opioid used to treat pain and as a cough suppressant.

This sudden bleeding into brain tissue or its ventricles is one of two major stroke categories, alongside the blockage-caused kind, and can trigger headache, one-sided weakness, or sudden speech and vision problems — what's the condition?
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), also known as hemorrhagic stroke, is a sudden bleeding into the tissues of the brain (i.e., the parenchyma), into its ventricles, or both.
Holder of 128 firearm patents, this American engineer invented the telescoping bolt that made compact autoloading pistols possible — who is he?

John Browning (January 23, 1855 - November 26, 1926) was an American firearm designer who developed many varieties of military and civilian firearms, cartridges, and gun mechanisms, many of which are still in use around the world.
First described in 1816 and classed in psychiatry as an impulse-control disorder, this condition is the inability to resist stealing items one doesn't even need — what's its name?
Kleptomania is the inability to resist the urge to steal items, usually for reasons other than personal use or financial gain.
Viruses muddy its definition, and it might exist beyond Earth in unfamiliar forms — but on this planet it fills air, water and soil, even harsh niches of extremophiles. What is it?
Life is the capacity, in matter, for processes such as cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, cell growth, adaptation, response to stimuli, and reproduction.
This alpha-amino acid, a building block for many proteins, carries a side chain that stays partially charged at the body's normal pH, classifying it among the basic amino acids — what is it?
Lysine (symbol Lys or K) is an -amino acid that is a precursor to many proteins.
This German-British theoretical physicist won a Nobel Prize for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics. Who is he?
Max Born (11 December 1882 - 5 January 1970) was a German-British theoretical physicist who was instrumental in the development of quantum mechanics.

This large-scale industrial activity extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and potash from the Earth, providing raw materials that can't be grown or feasibly manufactured — what is this activity called?
Mining is the extraction of geological materials and minerals from Earth's surface.
Named from the Ancient Greek for 'mouse's ear' after its foliage's shape, this genus of small blue Northern Hemisphere flowers serves as Alaska's official state flower — what's the genus?
Myosotis is a genus of flowering plants in the borage family Boraginaceae.

Introduced in 2001 and operated by the U.S. Air Force, this high-altitude, remotely piloted surveillance aircraft uses synthetic aperture radar and infrared sensors for long-endurance reconnaissance missions — name the aircraft?

Northrop Grumman RQ-4 Global Hawk is a high-altitude, remotely-piloted surveillance aircraft introduced in 2001. It was initially designed by Ryan Aeronautical (now part of Northrop Grumman), and known as Tier II+ during development.
It surges during childbirth and sexual activity, drives maternal bonding and milk production, and is released by the posterior pituitary — which hormone is this?
Oxytocin is a peptide hormone and neuropeptide normally produced in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary.

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.
This GABA-derived drug treats cognitive disorders, vertigo, and dyslexia, and shares its 'racetam' drug class with related compounds like levetiracetam and aniracetam — what is it?
Piracetam is a drug that has efficacy in cognitive disorders, vertigo, cortical myoclonus, dyslexia, and sickle cell anemia; sources differ on its usefulness for dementia.
Bloating, mood swings, breast tenderness and irritability that flare in the week or two before menstruation and fade once bleeding begins — what disruptive condition is this?
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a disruptive set of emotional and physical symptoms that regularly occur in the one to two weeks before the start of each menstrual period.
This colorless, odorless radioactive noble gas has the atomic number 86, and its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of under four days — name the element?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
This big, sociable black corvid is told apart from its relatives by a bare, whitish patch on its face, and it nests in noisy treetop colonies near farms and villages — which bird is it?
Rook (bird) (Corvus frugilegus) is a member of the family Corvidae in the passerine order of birds.
Caused by a lack of vitamin C, this deficiency disease shows up after about a month of poor diet with weakness, sore limbs, gum disease, and bleeding from the skin — what is it?
Scurvy is a deficiency disease (state of malnutrition) resulting from a lack of vitamin C (ascorbic acid).
Some of these organisms merge single cells into visible fruiting bodies via chemical signals called acrasins, aiding in the decay of vegetation — what group is this?
Slime mold (British) are a variety of small or microscopic organisms in different groups.
An English dyer and astronomer, this man's 1729 experiments were the first to systematically show that electricity could travel through metals and appear on the surface of insulators — who was he?
Stephen Gray (scientist) (December 1666 - February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
This genus of flowering plants in the daisy family is better known by the fluffy-seeded lawn weed it produces, with two European species now invasive nearly worldwide. What is it?
Taraxacum is a genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae which consists of species commonly known as dandelions.
Joining a tech giant in 1998 to run worldwide operations, this executive served as its COO before stepping up to CEO the day Steve Jobs resigned in 2011 — who is he?
Tim Cook (born November 1, 1960) is an American business executive who has served as the chief executive officer (CEO) of Apple since 2011.
What is the medical term for having dangerously high levels of urea in the blood, typically caused by kidney failure?

Uremia is the condition of having high levels of urea in the blood. It is the signs, symptoms and results from laboratory tests which result from inadequate excretory, regulatory, and endocrine function of the kidneys.
His 1925 Umdeutung paper reinterpreted old quantum theory, and two years later he published a famous uncertainty principle — which German physicist was he?

Werner Heisenberg (5 December 1901 - 1 February 1976) was a German theoretical physicist, one of the main pioneers of the theory of quantum mechanics and a principal scientist in the German nuclear program during World War II.
Also known as the empirical guideline, this statistical shorthand describes the percentage of values within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution — which one?
Transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly, this parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei is better known in humans as 'sleeping sickness' — what's its formal name?
African trypanosomiasis: Parasitic disease also known as sleeping sickness.

This exaggerated immune response occurs when the body mistakes a harmless substance for a threat, triggering histamine release from mast cells and conditions like hay fever or anaphylaxis. What is this reaction called?
Allergy: Immune system response to a substance that most people tolerate well.
Considered the father of the exact and natural sciences in Armenia, this 7th-century polymath wrote the first known Armenian geographic work — who was he?
When an injury to the wall of the body's main artery lets blood force its layers apart, victims often feel a sudden 'tearing' chest or back pain — what's this medical emergency called?
Aortic dissection: Injury to the innermost layer of the aorta.
About 200 times sweeter than table sugar, this artificial sweetener sold as NutraSweet and Equal had its FDA approval briefly revoked before being re-approved in 1981 — what is it?

Once the go-to sedatives and anticonvulsants, these barbituric-acid-derived depressants were largely replaced by benzodiazepines and 'Z-drugs' because of their high addiction and overdose risk — what class of drugs?
Barbiturate: Class of depressant drugs derived from barbituric acid.

With arms and tentacles up to 26 feet long held at right angles to its body, this deep-sea cephalopod has been spotted as deep as 6,212 meters — the only one of its kind known to survive the hadal zone. What is it?

Flying for the U.S. Air Force since 1955, this subsonic strategic bomber evolved from a six-turboprop straight-wing design into eight swept-wing turbojets and can haul up to 70,000 pounds of weapons — what's its name?
Boeing B-52 Stratofortress: American strategic bomber aircraft.

This Italian-American physicist invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to prove cosmic rays arrive more strongly from the West than the East, before Italy's racial laws forced him to flee — who was he?
Which multidrug-resistant fungal yeast colonizes skin in long-term care facilities and causes bloodstream infections with up to a 60% mortality rate?
Also known by the nickname 'catawba,' this genus of flowering trees is native to warm regions of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia — what genus is it?
Native to the mountains of Honduras and Guatemala and nicknamed the 'custard apple' for its creamy texture, this fruit was called 'the most delicious fruit known to men' by Mark Twain — which fruit?
Cherimoya: Edible fruit-bearing species of plant.
What is this — “Physiological phenomenon involving the engorgement of the clitoris”?

Clitoral erection: Physiological phenomenon involving the engorgement of the clitoris. Clitoral erection (also known as clitoral tumescence or female erection) is a physiological phenomenon where the clitoris becomes enlarged and firm.
One of the most intensively studied and intelligent cephalopods, this mollusk ranges from the Mediterranean and English coastline all the way to South Africa — which species?
Common octopus: Species of cephalopod. The common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) is a mollusk belonging to the class Cephalopoda.
These feather-gilled freshwater crustaceans share their taxonomic order with lobsters and turn up in everything from brooks to rice paddies — what are they?
Crayfish: Freshwater crustaceans. Crayfish are freshwater crustaceans belonging to the infraorder Astacidea, which also contains lobsters.
The first Western European combat aircraft to break Mach 2 in level flight, achieving the feat in October 1958, which French fighter jet family was this?
Dassault Mirage III: French supersonic fighter/interceptor aircraft.

Discovered in Arizona in the 1940s and first classified as a species of Megalosaurus, this theropod was reassigned to a new genus in 1970 once paleontologists noticed the twin crests on its skull — which dinosaur?
Dilophosaurus: Genus of theropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic.

Coined by Robert Spitzer in the late 1970s to replace the notion of a "depressive personality," this condition resembles major depression but lingers for at least two years — and now goes by "persistent depressive disorder." What was its original name?
Dysthymia: Psychiatric disorder defined by chronic depression.
Australia's tallest native bird, this flightless species can sprint up to 48 kilometers per hour and often goes weeks without drinking water — which bird?
Emu: Large flightless bird endemic to Australia.
Every animal, plant, fungus and seaweed belongs to this domain, defined by one shared cellular feature: a nucleus wrapped in its own membrane. What are they called?
Eukaryote: Domain of life whose cells have nuclei.
Made up mostly of undigested food broken down by gut bacteria, this bodily waste is expelled through the anus and can even be dried for fuel or used as fertilizer — what is it?
Feces: Solid or semisolid remains of undigested food.
Despite the name, these fifty species of rodent can't truly fly — they glide between trees using a furred membrane called a patagium. What are they?
Capable of living up to 177 years and weighing as much as 417 kilograms, which giant reptile — native to a chain of Pacific islands named for it — is the largest cold-blooded land animal alive today?
Galápagos tortoise: Species of reptile. The species comprises 15 subspecies (12 extant and 3 extinct).
The tallest land animal alive and the largest ruminant on Earth, its closest living relative is the okapi — which long-necked African mammal is it?

This algebraic structure — a set paired with an operation that's associative, has an identity element, and gives every member an inverse — is exemplified by the integers under addition. What is it called?

Group (mathematics): Set with associative invertible operation. The concept of a group was elaborated for handling, in a unified way, many mathematical structures such as numbers, geometric shapes and polynomial roots.

Often defined as the normal functioning of the body free of disease, pain, or injury, this multidimensional state of well-being can be promoted by exercise and sleep and harmed by smoking or stress — what's the one-word concept?
Health: Desirable level of functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being.
Also called urticaria, this skin condition brings red or flesh-colored raised, itchy bumps that may sting and often follow an allergic reaction — what is it?
Hives: Skin disease characterized by red, raised, and itchy bumps.
Defined as a blood level above 5.5 mmol/L, this elevated-potassium condition can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm and even cardiac arrest — what is it called?
Hyperkalemia: Excess potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels above 5.5 mmol/L defined as hyperkalemia.

ISO 56000:2020 defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — but the everyday version is the practical implementation of ideas, the cousin of invention focused on newness, improvement, and the spread of technologies. What's the word?
Innovation: Practical implementation of improvements. Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
Mentored by Louis Leakey, this English primatologist spent six decades at Gombe and revealed that chimpanzees use tools and form lasting social bonds — who was she?
Committed to accuracy and verification, this occupation and set of methods involves gathering and distributing the day's news — what field is it?
Journalism: Production of reports on current events.
Living as a recluse in a log house outside Kaluga, this Russian pioneer of rocket science inspired both Wernher von Braun and the architects of the Soviet space program — who is he?

Native to the dry grasslands and deserts of Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, and Nepal, this ground-dwelling reptile is so widely captive-bred it's considered the first domesticated species of its kind — what is it?
Leopard gecko: Species of reptile. The leopard gecko is a popular pet, and due to extensive captive breeding it is sometimes referred to as the first domesticated species of lizard.

This American stealth strike fighter comes in three flavors — conventional, short-takeoff/vertical-landing, and carrier-based — and with 883 in service is the world's fourth-most-numerous military aircraft. What is it?

Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II: American stealth multirole fighter aircraft. The Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is an American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters.
With the formula MgCl2, this colorless salt forms hydrates and serves as the principal precursor to large-scale production of its namesake metal — what is it?
Magnesium chloride: Inorganic salt: MgCl2 and its hydrates. It forms hydrates MgCl2·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 12.
Part of the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family, some species in this plant genus share the common name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Discovered in 1893 and existing as two mirror-image enantiomers, this CNS stimulant is best known in its hydrochloride-salt form nicknamed 'crystal' — what is it?
Medically termed a 'spontaneous abortion,' this is the loss of an embryo or fetus before it can survive independently — distinct from a stillbirth, which occurs after 20 weeks. What is it?
Miscarriage: Natural premature termination of pregnancy.

Made of contractile proteins called actin and myosin, this soft tissue exists in three vertebrate forms — skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — and forms during a developmental process called myogenesis — what is it?
Muscle: Important Biological tissue that allows movement.
The sole species in its genus and a fixture of Mediterranean gardens, this drought-and-flood-tolerant shrub of the dogbane family is also called rose laurel or rosebay — what is it?
Nerium: Species of plant. It is the only species currently classified in the genus Nerium, belonging to subfamily Apocynoideae of the dogbane family Apocynaceae.
The largest structure inside a eukaryotic cell's nucleus, this site of ribosome assembly also helps form signal recognition particles and responds to cellular stress — what is it?
Nucleolus: Largest structure in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. The nucleolus also participates in the formation of signal recognition particles and plays a role in the cell's response to stress.

This vertebrate clade has skeletons made mostly of bone rather than cartilage, and includes both classic 'bony fish' and, cladistically, every land vertebrate descended from lobe-finned ancestors — what is it?
Osteichthyes: Diverse clade of vertebrate animals.
Named from the Latin word for 'sparrow,' this bird order — making up over half of all species — is defined by perching feet with three toes forward and one back. What's it called?
Passerine: Perching birds of the order Passeriformes.
Who is this — “Danish entrepreneur and murderer”?
Peter Madsen: Danish entrepreneur and murderer. Peter Langkjær Madsen (Danish: [ˈpʰe̝ˀtɐ ˈlɑŋˌkʰeˀɐ̯ ˈmæsn̩]; born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur.
This scientific term covers walruses, sea lions, and true seals — fin-footed marine mammals whose closest living relatives are weasels and raccoons — what is the term?
Pinniped: Taxonomic group of semi-aquatic mammals.

A colorless salt that looks unnervingly like sugar but tastes acrid and bitter, this compound is mostly used in gold mining and electroplating — and just 200 to 300 milligrams will kill nearly any human. What is it?
Potassium cyanide: Chemical compound. It is a colorless salt, similar in appearance to sugar, that is highly soluble in water.

Also known as talk therapy, this practice uses regular personal interaction to help people change behavior and improve well-being, with effects research suggests often outlast those of medication — what is it called?
Psychotherapy: Clinically applied psychology for desired behavior change.

Distinguished from its smaller cousin mainly by size rather than any strict taxonomy, this long-tailed rodent genus numbers 56 known species, with 'kangaroo' and 'bandicoot' variants named for their appearance — which rodent?
This blue supergiant in Orion, also known as Beta Orionis, outshines the Sun by up to 363,000 times and anchors a system of at least four stars — which star?
Rigel: Brightest star in the constellation Orion.
Named after the Latin word for willow tree, from which it was first derived, this plant hormone and aspirin precursor shows up in anti-acne cosmetics — what is it?
Salicylic acid: Chemical compound used in medicines and industry.
These marine algae include the kelps that shelter fisheries and are estimated to produce at least half of Earth's oxygen — what are they collectively called?
Seaweed: Macroscopic marine algae. Seaweed, or macroalgae, refers to thousands of species of macroscopic, multicellular, marine algae.

This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship for an unmatched 54 years, leaving his name on equations of fluid mechanics and a theorem of vector calculus — who is it?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet: British mathematician and physicist (1819–1903)
This family of roughly 1,450 moths flies so swiftly on narrow wings and streamlined bodies that some species hover at flowers and are routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what's its scientific name?
